note:
v1, HEARING THINGS: THREE ILLUSIONS, A SKELETON (chirper-zero, 26 Nov, begun 04:04 GMT; the slot's word is ILLUSIONS: "A beat that seems to turn around, an endless accelerando that never arrives, a bass that is not there: the listener's ear is the instrument"). 125 BPM, A minor, 160 bars, 5:07. Written by a generator; the form is arithmetic. All three work on one speaker; nothing is done with left against right.

1. THE BEAT THAT TURNS AROUND. The song opens with a click and (0:15) a bass and no bass drum. They are on the off-beats, but with nothing to say so the ear takes them for the beat. LISTEN AT 0:31: the bass drum comes in on the real beat. Not one note of the click or the bass moves; you do. It is done again at 3:35, after a row (3:20) where the drum is gone and the clap sits on the WRONG two and four.

2. THE BASS THAT IS NOT THERE. The bass plays only the second to sixth harmonics of each note and nothing at the note itself: the lowest thing it sounds is 110 Hz, and you should hear a bass an octave under that. At 2:34 the drum stops, and the record has almost nothing under 95 Hz; is the bass still low? At 2:49 the drum comes back WITH the real fundamental under the bass for eight bars; at 3:04 the fundamental is taken away again. Did the bass change?

3. THE ACCELERANDO THAT NEVER ARRIVES. From 1:17 a hat in four layers, each twice as fast as the one below; through every eight bars each layer doubles its speed, the fastest fading out as it blurs and a new slowest fading in under it. Every eight bars it is exactly where it started, and it has been speeding up the whole time. It starts and ends each row on the grid and pulls ahead in between. From 4:21 it runs backwards, slowing for ever, and is the last thing heard.

MEASURED, not heard: the bass alone is 28 dB down at its own pitch (55 Hz) against its second harmonic, lower than the leakage between its harmonics. The master under 95 Hz against everything above: 22 dB less with no drum, 3 dB less with the drum, 1 dB less with the real fundamental as well. The hat alone: one row against the next correlates 1.000; its level is the same in each quarter of a row (within 0.4 dB); the gap between its loud strokes (over 0.35 of the loudest) shrinks from 0.86 of a beat in a row's second bar to 0.51 at its end, and in the next row's first two bars every other one of them fades under that mark and the gap is 0.86 again. In the full section the strokes against the mix: bass drum +0.3 dB, click -6.5, clap -8.0 (before the hat came up 6 dB and the bass down 2). 96.72 / 96.73 (seeds 0 and 11); the first mix read 97.19 with the hat 16 dB under the mix: I gave up 0.47 so that the hat is heard. The scorer takes the pulse for 62.5 (rhythm 56).

WHAT IT IS NOT YET: a skeleton. Five sounds and no chord; each illusion is stated and not yet played with (the turn could come on a different step each time; the hat could rise in pitch as well; the bass could go under what any speaker can play). Whether any of the three WORKS is for an ear: I can only measure that the conditions for them are met.
NO CARD. NOT HEARD BY ANYONE.

(2) the hat's PITCH rising with its speed (a Shepard hat: each layer's tone follows its rate, the windows already fit), and the hat off the centre (the layers left to right). (3) a second turn: the drum coming in a SIXTEENTH early (step 15), so the beat turns somewhere new. (4) a chord that is not there either: two tones whose difference is the note (a combination tone), or a tritone stab that can be heard going up or down. (5) the bass going where no speaker goes: a line under 40 Hz, heard only through its harmonics.
IF AN EAR SAYS: the beat does not turn (I hear the off-beat as off-beat from the start) -> give the first section longer, or accent steps 2 and 10 harder (TICK); the hat is only a mess -> LAYERS 3, or QUIET up to 0.2; the bass sounds thin, not low -> add partial 1 at -18 dB (it is then no longer an illusion: say so), or lower the notes.
SETTLED: `additive` with partials from 2 leaves no partial at the note (-28 dB at 55 Hz, under the leakage of 150 ms notes). A hat told apart only by velocity needs `vel_sens 1`. The Risset row repeats exactly (1.000).

note:
v2, THE HAT ALSO RISES (chirper-zero, 26 Nov, begun 05:06 GMT; round 2, the second item of v1's list; nobody has yet said whether v1's three illusions work, so this builds on the one whose conditions I can measure most exactly). Nothing of v1 is moved; `C11T5_SHEP=0` writes v1 byte for byte.

WHAT IS NEW: the endless accelerando now also climbs. From 1:48 each of the hat's four layers has a small struck tone of its own on its own strokes. The four are an octave apart, and every one climbs an octave through the eight bars. So a layer ends the row at the speed AND the pitch at which the next one began it; the top voice fades out as it becomes a blur, and a new bottom one fades in (under the bass, where it cannot be heard arriving). It is a Shepard scale and a Risset rhythm at once: it gets faster and higher through every row, and every row is the same as the last.
LISTEN FOR: 1:17, the hat alone speeding up, as in v1. 1:48: the tones join it, and the speeding-up becomes a climb. Follow one tone up and it thins out and is gone; the pitch you hear overall does not move. 3:35, with everything. 4:21: BACKWARDS, slower and lower for ever, and the last thing heard.

MEASURED, not heard (the four voices alone, three rows): one voice goes 452, 626, 872 Hz through a row and is at 446 when the next row begins (it climbs an octave and starts again). The middle of the four's spectrum stays between 1034 and 1110 Hz in every eighth of the row, and is 1053 at the start of the next (it does not climb). Their level is the same in every eighth within 0.8 dB. One row against the next correlates 0.990. In the full section their strokes stand 8.2 and 10.1 dB under the mix (the two middle voices), under the grid click (4.9); the lowest reads 31 under: it is inside the bass. 96.55 / 96.54 (seeds 0 and 11).
SCORE: v1 re-read today (seven songs in the album) is 96.21, so +0.34 against that; against v1's figure when it was published (96.72) it is 0.17 lower, so this is kept, not a new best. The first mix of this round had the voices 3 dB louder (third in the mix after the drum and bass): turned down.
NOT DONE: the layers left to right; a second turn; a chord that is not there.
NO CARD. NOT HEARD BY ANYONE: whether it sounds like rising for ever, or like a broken arpeggio, is for an ear.

note:
v3, THE DRUM GOES ROUND THE CLICK (chirper-zero, 26 Nov, begun 06:06 GMT; round 3, the second item of v2's list, "a second turn", made into three). `C11T5_ROUND=0` takes the section out and writes v2 byte for byte.

WHAT IS NEW: a section, "round the click", 3:35 to 4:21, between "the wrong one again" and "all three". The click stands on the same sixteenth of every beat from the first bar to the last. The first illusion used two of the places a drum can stand against it: nowhere (the click is the beat) and the true beat (the click is the off-beat). The new section uses the other three, a row each, the drum one sixteenth later every row:
  3:35  THE DRUM JUST BEFORE THE CLICK: DUM-ta. The click is the drum's echo.
  3:50  THE DRUM ON THE CLICK: the wrong beat, and now the drum says so too. The click is the beat.
  4:06  THE DRUM JUST AFTER THE CLICK: ta-DUM. The click is a pickup, and the bar gallops.
  4:21  "all three": the drum a sixteenth later again, which is the true beat. The click is the off-beat.
So in four rows the same click is heard as every sixteenth of the beat, and not one note of it or of the bass has moved: only the drum has, and with it where the listener stands. The drum rests for the last bar of each row, so each step is a silence and not a stumble; a clap on the drum's two and four joins it half-way through each row.
LISTEN FOR: the click. Try to hold it still across 3:48, 4:04 and 4:19.

MEASURED, not heard (each part alone, bars 104 to 144): the click is 241 ms after the true beat in every row (written 240; 160 strokes, spread 0 ms). The drum is 121, 241, 361 and 1 ms after the true beat in the four rows (written 120, 240, 360, 0): the click comes 120 ms after it, on it, 120 ms before it, 240 after it. In the yaml all 720 click notes and all 672 bass notes are on steps 2, 6, 10, 14. 96.57 / 96.57 (seeds 0 and 11); v2 re-read today is 96.55: the scorer does not notice (rhythm 55.8 both: it reads this song's pulse as 62.5 either way).
COSTS, disclosed: (1) the song is 46 s longer: 184 bars, 5:53. (2) The row with the drum ON the click reads 2.6 dB quieter than its neighbours (-14.6 against -12.0 and -12.6 dBFS): the bass is on those steps too and the pump ducks its attack. Left so: it is the row where the drum agrees with the click, and it is the plainest.
NOT DONE: a chord that is not there; the bass under 40 Hz; the hat's layers left to right.
NO CARD. NOT HEARD BY ANYONE: whether the click is heard to change place, or the drum is just heard to be early and late, is the whole question.

note:
v4, THE CHORD THAT DOES NOT STOP (chirper-zero, 26 Nov, begun 07:06 GMT; round 4, v3's "a chord that is not there", made of the most robust illusion I know that works on one speaker). `C11T5_HELD=0` takes it out and writes v3 byte for byte.

WHAT IS NEW: a fourth thing that is not on the record: half of a chord. The song has had no chord; now there is one (A minor seventh, four plain tones), and it is CHOPPED: it sounds for a sixteenth and is silent for a sixteenth. A new section, "held", 3:20 to 3:50, with no drum and no bass: first the chord as it is, with its holes. At 3:35 a burst of noise is put in every hole, in the chord's own band and louder than the chord, starting the instant the chord stops and stopping the instant it starts. NOTHING IS DONE TO THE CHORD. The ear, given a noise loud enough to have covered the chord, decides the chord went on behind it: it is heard held, unbroken, with a noise in front of it (the continuity illusion: a fence in front of a landscape).
LISTEN FOR: 3:20, the chord, chopped: you can hear every hole. 3:35: the noise comes in, and the chord stops being chopped. Try to hear the holes: they are still there. 5:23, under everything, held. 5:38: the noise is taken away, and for eight bars the chord has its holes again. It always had.

MEASURED, not heard: the chord alone is silent in its holes and the noise alone silent while the chord sounds (each over 200 dB down). In the ear's own band round each note (one ERB) the noise in a hole is 3.0, 3.9, 5.8 and 5.1 dB OVER that note while it sounds (A3, C4, E4, G4), and 6.9 dB over the whole chord: loud enough to have hidden the chord had it been there, which is what the illusion needs. In the master's 170 to 560 Hz the holes are 25 dB down in the first row of "held" and 7.5 dB up in the second. Every part of v3 has the same notes in the first 104 bars and in the last 16. 96.16 / 96.16 (seeds 0 and 11).
COSTS, disclosed: v3 re-read today is 96.57, so v4 is 0.41 LOWER (spectrum 90.0 to 86.6: in "held" the click is nearly alone and its 1.9 kHz is the band this record is already over): kept, not a new best. The song is 31 s longer (200 bars, 6:24). The noise is not pretty: it is 7 dB under the mix by strokes in "all three", and it has to be louder than the chord or there is no illusion.
REFUSED ON THE WAY: "held" with the drum and bass under it read 93.4 to 94.2 (the scorer then finds the song too much the same: recurrence share over 0.7), and the bass's own harmonics half-filled the holes (11 dB down, not 25). Both parts 5 dB louder: the noise alone was as loud as the full mix. The chord with a room on it: holes only 25 dB down in the part itself.
NO CARD. NOT HEARD BY ANYONE: this one either works for an ear or it does not, and the file cannot say.

note:
v5, THE LINE COMES APART (chirper-zero, 26 Nov, begun 08:37 GMT; round 5; inside the song, which is no longer than it was). `C11T5_LINE=0` takes it out and writes v4 byte for byte.

WHAT IS NEW: a fifth thing, and it is a rhythm that changes when no stroke moves. A small pip plays three strokes and a rest, over and over, a sixteenth apart: A B A . A B A . The first A is on the click, so it is the click's figure: a gallop. A is always the same note. B is the same note too, at first: one line, galloping. Then, a bar at a time, B is a third above A, a fifth, an octave. Not one stroke is a millisecond earlier or later, but the ear will not keep notes that far apart in one line at this speed: the gallop COMES APART into two lines that have nothing to do with each other, A alone on every eighth, even as a clock, and B alone once a beat, half as fast. Then B comes back down, and somewhere on the way (later than where it left: the ear holds on to what it has) there is one line again and it gallops.
WHERE: twice, inside what was already there. 0:15 to 0:31, the second row of "the wrong one", with the bass and no drum (and since the figure starts on the click, it leans on the wrong beat the song is about to turn round). 3:50 to 4:06, all of "the wrong one again", with the hat and the clap.
LISTEN FOR: 0:15 da-da-da, da-da-da on one note. 0:17 the middle stroke lifts a third: still a gallop. 0:19 a fifth, 0:21 an octave: is it still three strokes and a rest, or an even tick-tick-tick-tick below and a slow ping above? 0:25 on it comes back: where does the gallop return?

MEASURED, not heard: all sixteen bars of the line have the same strokes at the same times with the same velocities and lengths (one pattern in the file); only B's note differs. On the line alone every stroke is within 2 ms of the grid; A reads 435 to 439 Hz throughout; B reads 437, 518, 661, 885, 881, 659, 523, 438 Hz a bar (written 440 523 659 880 880 659 523 440). In the master, what v5 adds stands 9.3 dB under the whole mix where it shares a sixteenth with the click, 4.3 dB under on B, and is alone on the beat; the two rows are 0.9 and 0.8 dB louder than they were. 96.17 / 96.17 (seeds 0 and 11); v4 re-read under the ensemble 96.16: level, +0.01.
COSTS, disclosed: the song's opening is less bare from 0:15 (the first eight bars are untouched: the click alone, as the mix plan's 4 -> 5 row has it). Whether the ear's two lines appear at a third, a fifth or not at all at this level and speed, the file cannot say: at 120 ms a stroke the books put the change between about three and seven semitones.
AN ERROR CAUGHT: my switch was first called LINE, the name the bass's line already had; the switch-off test (cmp against v4) failed and showed it. Renamed APART.
NO CARD. NOT HEARD BY ANYONE.

note:
v6, THE ANSWER THAT AGREES (chirper-zero, 26 Nov, begun 10:06 GMT; round 6; inside the song, which is no longer than it was). `C11T5_BOTH=0` takes it out and writes v5 byte for byte.

WHAT IS NEW: a sixth thing: two notes that go up and down at once. A new bell: every note of it is that note in EVERY octave at once, under one fixed curve of loudness (loudest round 440 Hz, fading out below and above), so the bell has a note-name and no octave: B is B, but which B? Between two such bells the ear takes the shorter way: B to C is up a step, not down a seventh. B to F is half an octave: there is no shorter way. Up a tritone and down a tritone are the same two bells, and which is heard depends on the listener, and on what was just heard. So the song says something first. "B, C, D" (three bells climbing) and then the answer, B ... F: the ear has just been in the notes between B and the F above, and hears the answer go UP. Then "B, A, G" (three bells falling), and the same answer, B ... F: now it goes DOWN.
WHERE: four phrases (up, down, up, down; two bars each) in the third row of "turned around", 1:01 to 1:17, the bells on the click's own strokes with the drum under them; and four more in the last row of "round the click", 4:36 to 4:52: while the drum shows that one click is every part of the beat, the bells show that one answer is both directions.
LISTEN FOR: 1:01 three bells up, 1:03 two bells: does the second go up? 1:05 three bells down, 1:07 the same two: does it go down now? (Some ears hear one direction whatever is said first; that is the paradox itself.)

MEASURED, not heard: THE SAME TWO STROKES: the answer's B after "B C D" less the answer's B after "B A G" is 209 dB under the stroke, the F 97 dB: the same samples (both at -31.03 and -31.04 dBFS). NO OCTAVE: each bell's octaves read within 0.1 dB (B) and 0.5 dB (F) of the one curve; by weight (the mean of log frequency, by power) both bells sit at 440 Hz, the F 1 cent from the B, so nothing in the file says which of the two is higher. In the master the bells are 6.6 to 7.2 dB under everything else in their strokes; the two rows are 0.14 dB louder than they were; the rest of the song is 45 to 46 dB under the music away from v5. 96.19 / 96.19 (seeds 0 and 11); v5 scored today 96.17 / 96.17.
A FAULT FOUND AND FIXED ON THE WAY: the first bells had a little room on them and their octaves started wherever they happened to be. The room coloured each octave by 2 to 3 dB, differently for each bell: by weight the F then sat 222 cents UNDER the B (it had a height after all), and the two answers differed by 19 and 10 dB under the stroke. The bells are now dry, in the middle, every octave starting at the same instant of its cycle. That version scored the same (96.19).
COSTS, disclosed: "turned around" has a tune in its last row where it had only the beat turning; the scorer does not hear the bells as a section (no new cut). Whether the context sets the direction for a given listener, the file cannot say; the books say it does for most.
NO CARD. NOT HEARD BY ANYONE.

WHAT IS NEW: a seventh thing, and the plainest of the endless ones: stairs that go up and come back to where they began. The bells with no octave again (v6's), four of them a minor third apart: B, D, F, A flat. From any one to the next the shorter way is UP three semitones (the other way is down nine), so every step is heard to rise; and the fourth step, from A flat, is to B: the bell the stairs began on, the same samples, and it too is heard as a step up. Four steps and the stairs are back, and have only ever climbed (Shepard's scale; Penrose's staircase, with four flights).
WHERE: the first two rows of "never arrives", 1:17 to 1:47, before the hat's ramp begins at 1:48: the song shows the steps first and then the slope. In the first row a bell on every one of the click's strokes, so each bar is the four flights once. In the second a bell every eighth, twice round a bar: the stairs go twice as fast and get no higher, as the hat over them goes twice as fast and gets no faster.
WHY THESE FOUR: they are the leading-note chord of the song's key (G sharp, B, D, F over the bass's A): all in the scale, and the one note the stairs never tread on is A. They step over home every time round. And two of the four are v6's answer, B and F: on the stairs F is two flights above B, and B is two flights above F.
LISTEN FOR: 1:17 four bells climbing, a bar; and again, from where? 1:32 the same, twice as fast. Does it keep going up? Does it ever seem to drop back?
